name: Azure Data Box
oneLiner: Offline and online bulk data transfer of large datasets into Azure.
whatItIs: Azure Data Box is Microsoft's family of solutions for moving large datasets into Azure when the network isn't practical. The flagship is the offline path: Microsoft ships you a ruggedised physical storage appliance, you copy data onto it locally at LAN speed, ship it back, and Azure ingests it into your storage — the fastest way to move tens or hundreds of terabytes when uploading over the internet would take weeks. The family spans Data Box (the appliance), Data Box Disk, and Data Box Heavy, plus online options (Data Box Gateway / Azure Storage Mover / AzCopy) for network transfer. It's the bulk on-ramp that seeds an Azure data lake with existing archives.

inPractice.narrative: A company has 200 TB of historical files on-prem to move into ADLS, but their internet link would take months to upload it. They order an Azure Data Box appliance, copy the data onto it over the local network in days, and ship it back to Microsoft, who loads it into their Azure storage account. For ongoing, smaller syncs afterward they switch to an online tool like AzCopy or Storage Mover. Data Box is the offline bulk on-ramp for the initial heavy lift into the Azure lake.

coreConcepts.detail: For datasets too big for the network, Microsoft ships a physical device you fill locally and return; Azure ingests it — trading transit time for not saturating your link for weeks.
Data Box (~terabytes-scale appliance), Data Box Disk (smaller, SSDs), and Data Box Heavy (very large) match different data volumes.
Data Box Gateway, Azure Storage Mover and AzCopy handle network-based transfer and ongoing sync — the counterpart to the offline appliances.
Data is encrypted on the device (AES-256); the appliance is ruggedised and tamper-resistant, and wiped after ingestion per NIST guidelines.
Ingests into Azure Blob/ADLS, seeding the data lake or migrating file archives into managed storage.
The rule of thumb: if uploading over your available bandwidth would take longer than shipping a device, go offline; otherwise use an online tool.

whenToUse: One-time migration of very large datasets (10s–100s of TB+) into Azure.
Seeding an ADLS data lake where network upload would take weeks/months.
Sites with limited or unreliable internet bandwidth.
Bulk archive/backup relocation into Azure storage.
Initial heavy lift, then switching to online sync afterwards.
whenNotToUse: Ongoing incremental sync — use AzCopy/Storage Mover (online) instead.
Database migration/replication — use Azure Database Migration Service.
Real-time event/stream ingestion — that's Event Hubs.
Smaller datasets that upload comfortably over the network.

keyFacts.label: Role
keyFacts.value: Bulk data transfer into Azure — offline (appliance) and online.

keyFacts.label: Offline devices
keyFacts.value: Data Box, Data Box Disk, Data Box Heavy.

keyFacts.label: Online tools
keyFacts.value: Data Box Gateway, Storage Mover, AzCopy.

keyFacts.label: Security
keyFacts.value: AES-256 encryption; ruggedised, wiped after ingest.

pricingShape: For the offline appliances, Data Box bills a per-device service fee for the order (plus extra daily fees if you keep it beyond the included window) and shipping — a bounded, one-time migration cost. Online options like AzCopy are essentially free tooling where you pay the underlying storage and any egress. Destination Azure storage is billed separately. The economics question is transit time vs bandwidth: for network-impractical volumes the flat device fee beats weeks of throttled upload; for modest data, online transfer avoids the device fee entirely.
gotchas: It's mainly for one-time bulk moves — for ongoing sync, switch to AzCopy/Storage Mover.
Keeping the device beyond the included window accrues daily fees — copy and return promptly.
Physical shipping adds days/weeks of transit — factor it into migration timelines.
It moves files/objects, not databases — use Database Migration Service for those.
Choosing the wrong device size (Disk vs Box vs Heavy) means multiple trips or wasted capacity — size to the dataset.

equivalents.name: AWS DataSync
equivalents.note: Online bulk transfer; AWS Snow family is the offline-appliance counterpart to Data Box.

equivalents.name: Storage Transfer Service
equivalents.note: Online bulk transfer into Cloud Storage; Transfer Appliance is the offline counterpart.
